There is no single \'best\' stack for every game. Device, Android version, container/fork, game engine and the exact build all matter. EmuHub packages can come from third-party catalogs, so always match the component to the environment that will use it.
Recent stable Turnip first; test Qualcomm if a game has driver-specific issues.

Pick the provider EmuHub should use for this category. Your choice is remembered.
Turnip is Mesa\'s open-source Vulkan driver for Qualcomm Adreno GPUs. In Android Windows-gaming environments it is commonly used underneath DXVK or VKD3D to provide Vulkan acceleration.

Start with a recent stable Turnip build that explicitly supports your Adreno generation. The newest build is a good starting point, but it is not automatically the fastest or most compatible for every game.
A strong default for most Adreno devices, especially when the game relies on Vulkan through DXVK or VKD3D.
Try Qualcomm or an older known-good Turnip build if a game crashes, has missing textures, shader corruption, broken lighting, or gets worse after a driver update.
Compare drivers with the same game settings and the same save/scene.
Stable builds are safer for daily use; experimental builds can fix newer games but may introduce regressions.
A driver that is best for one game may be worse for another.

Qualcomm packages are proprietary Adreno graphics drivers originating from Qualcomm/vendor software. They use a different driver stack from Mesa Turnip and can behave very differently from game to game.
Use Turnip as the general starting point, then test a Qualcomm build when the game has a Turnip-specific problem or when a known recommendation exists for your GPU and Android version.
Games or devices that show better compatibility, rendering, or performance with the vendor driver stack.
Return to Turnip if you see startup failures, Vulkan feature errors, visual corruption, or noticeably worse frame pacing.
Driver compatibility is tied closely to the GPU generation and device software.
Do not assume a higher package number is always better for your phone.
Keep a known-good Turnip build available as a fallback.

Wine is a compatibility layer that translates Windows API calls into calls understood by the host operating system. Wine itself is not a CPU emulator; on ARM64 it is commonly combined with Box64, FEX, WoW64/ARM64EC components, or similar translation technology.
Use a recent stable or known-good Wine build that is supported by the container or launcher you are using. Prefer compatibility over chasing the highest version number.
Windows applications and games that need a general-purpose Windows runtime, especially outside a Steam-specific Proton setup.
Try a different Wine build, staging/custom build, or Proton-based runtime when a game requires patches that your current Wine build does not include.
Changing Wine can affect an existing prefix, so keep backups for important containers.
New Wine releases can fix APIs while also changing behaviour in older games.
The Wine build must match the architecture strategy used by your container.

Proton is Valve\'s gaming compatibility tool built around Wine plus additional gaming-focused components and patches. Official Proton targets Steam on Linux; Android/Winlator catalogs may provide adapted or custom packages rather than the exact official Steam package.

When your container supports Proton packages, start with a stable or widely tested build. Use Experimental, GE, or other custom variants when a specific game needs their fixes rather than assuming they are universally faster.
Windows games that benefit from gaming-specific Wine patches and a pre-integrated compatibility stack.
Use plain Wine when the application is not gaming-focused, when a Proton package is incompatible with your container, or when an older known-good runtime works better.
Proton is based on Wine; it is not a separate CPU emulator.
A Proton build that is excellent for one title can regress another.
Check whether the downloaded package is intended for your specific Android container/fork.
x86_64 Linux user-space translation on ARM64

Box64 runs x86_64 Linux programs on non-x86_64 systems such as ARM64 and uses dynamic recompilation plus native-library bridges to improve performance. In Android Windows-gaming stacks it can be one of the layers that makes x64 Wine and related binaries usable on ARM phones.
Use the stable/current build recommended by your container. Leave advanced dynarec options at their defaults first, then tune only when a particular game needs it.
Power users and containers that are designed around Box64, with broad per-game tuning options and frequent ARM64 gaming use.
Try FEXCore or another Box64 build if you hit CPU-emulation crashes, severe stutter, unsupported instructions, or a known game-specific regression.
Box64 settings can trade compatibility for speed, so change one option at a time.
The newest nightly may improve performance but can also regress a game.
CPU translation and GPU-driver choice are separate layers; both can affect the final result.
Box64 build for Wine WoW64 workflows

WOWBox64 is Box64\'s WoW64-oriented build path, producing a wowbox64.dll for Wine/Hangover-style workflows. It is designed for environments that intentionally use this architecture rather than as a drop-in replacement for normal Box64.
Only choose WOWBox64 when your container or Wine setup explicitly supports or requests it. For a conventional Box64-based container, use regular Box64 instead.
WoW64/ARM64-oriented setups that are specifically built around wowbox64.dll and want to reduce unnecessary translation boundaries.
Use regular Box64 or FEXCore if the container is not designed for WOWBox64, or if the WoW64 path introduces compatibility issues.
Treat WOWBox64 as an advanced component, not a generic \'faster Box64\'.
Its usefulness depends heavily on how the Wine/container package was built.
Keep the CPU translator matched to the runtime architecture used by the container.
FEX is a fast user-mode x86 and x86-64 emulator for ARM64 Linux. It can work alongside Wine or Proton and can forward graphics API calls to native host libraries to reduce some emulation overhead.
Use FEXCore when your container explicitly supports it. Compare it with Box64 on the actual game rather than choosing only by benchmark or version number.
Containers that support FEX and games that behave better with its translation model; it also offers a different compatibility path from Box64.
Try Box64 when a game has instability, missing instruction support, worse performance, or when the container has stronger Box64 integration.
FEX and Box64 solve similar CPU-architecture problems in different ways.
There is no universal winner; game engine, container and device all matter.
Use the runtime recommended by the container as your baseline before experimenting.
DXVK translates Direct3D 8, 9, 10 and 11 calls to Vulkan. Wine/Proton can then run many Windows games while the Vulkan driver, such as Turnip, handles the GPU work.
For a DirectX 9/10/11 game, start with a recent stable DXVK build supported by your Vulkan driver. If a new version breaks a title, test the previous known-good release.
Most DirectX 8–11 games where the device has a capable Vulkan driver.
Use VKD3D for DirectX 12. For very old Direct3D games, D7VK or WineD3D may fit better. Use an older/compatible DXVK branch if your Vulkan driver lacks features required by newer DXVK versions.
DXVK performance depends heavily on the underlying Vulkan driver.
Shader compilation stutter and a low average FPS are different problems; test long enough for caches to warm up.
If the game supports multiple renderers, make sure you know which DirectX version it is actually using.
VKD3D-Proton implements Direct3D 12 on top of Vulkan and is the main D3D12 path used by Proton-style gaming stacks. It relies on modern Vulkan features, so GPU-driver quality matters a lot.
For a DirectX 12 game, use a recent stable VKD3D-Proton build together with a recent compatible Vulkan driver. Keep a known-good older build if you experiment with nightlies.
DirectX 12 games. It is not a replacement for DXVK when the game is using D3D11 or older APIs.
If the game offers DirectX 11 and D3D12 is unstable or slower on your device, try the game\'s DX11 mode with DXVK. Also test a different Vulkan driver when rendering issues appear.
D3D12 tends to depend on newer Vulkan features more aggressively than older DirectX translation paths.
Turnip/Qualcomm choice can materially change VKD3D behaviour.
Use the game\'s native DX11/DX12 selector when available for clean comparisons.
D7VK is a Vulkan-based translation layer for very old Direct3D APIs, including Direct3D 7, 6, 5 and 3. It is aimed at older Windows games that predate the APIs normally handled by modern DXVK.
Use D7VK when you know the game uses an old Direct3D 3–7 renderer. For games that mix DirectDraw, GDI and old D3D in unusual ways, WineD3D can still be the better fallback.
Classic Windows games using old Direct3D immediate-mode renderers.
Try WineD3D or an alternative renderer if the game has broken menus, 2D overlays, videos, or other DirectDraw/GDI interoperability problems.
Do not use D7VK simply because a game is old; first identify the renderer it uses.
Some old games offer OpenGL or Glide renderers that may work better.
Legacy games often need game-specific fixes beyond the graphics translation layer.
